To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The volume of urea clearance (Kt) is a useful metric to guide therapy prescription for more frequent HD.
the dialysate volume is a reasonable proxy for Kt in more frequent HD.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new method for the synthesis of urea derivatives and their application to the synthesis of biologically active compounds.

the development of a new generation of urea‐based dialysis therapy dosing guides that are based on urea clearance and that are applicable to a variety of HD delivery systems and dialysis schedules, including more frequent HD.

the study of the chemical reactions of urea with the aim of obtaining information on the mechanism of the reaction, the rate constants of the elementary steps and the rate constants of some of the overall steps of the reaction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the volume of dialysate used is the best guide to prescribe for more frequent hemodiafiltration (HF).
the volume of dialysis fluid is a more accurate measure of small solute removal than Kt.
the urea reduction ratio is a poor surrogate of small solute clearance, and the volume of ureas cleared is a better surrogate of small soluteclearance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the urea Kt is an excellent dosing guide for prescribing more frequent HD.
we found that the volume of Urea Cleared (VUC) can be used as a therapy dosimetry guide for more frequent HD.
the dialysate volume prescribed for more frequent HD is a reasonable estimate of the volume of ureas cleared and, thus, of small solute removal.
The main takeaway from our work is that
dialysis dose should be based on Kt, and the dialysate volume should be based on a target Kt.
the volume of dialysate used is an important determinant of the urea clearance achieved during a dialysis treatment.
dialysate volumes prescribed for more frequent hemodiafiltration (HDF) are not sufficient to clear urea at the same rate as conventional thrice weekly hemodialysis.
